title: profiling-request-spiking-latency-during-batch-warmup
body:
TL;DR: Intermittent p95/p99 spikes at the start of batch waves (observed under synthetic ramp tests and two customer incidents) are dominated by CPU-side work in the request handshake and Python-level JSON/tokenization paths. The pattern is a warmup spike: the first ~200ms after a traffic increase shows heavy single-thread CPU time, causing queuing and tail latency even though GPU model latency is steady.

Context and why I care:
- Two recent customer reports (both low-concurrency but bursty; ~50->300 RPS bursts) showed 3x-6x p95 regressions for ~5s after each spike.
- Host-level metrics showed CPU oscillation while GPU remained underutilized.
- We need to understand whether this is a serving runtime issue (request parsing/tokenization/threading) vs upstream (client sends big headers / malformed bodies).

Hypotheses:
1) JSON parsing + request validation in Python is single-threaded and blocks request threads during burst startup.
2) Tokenizer warm-up (first time loading regexes / bpe caches) uses Python globals and acquires GIL for longer than expected.
3) Threadpool starvation at the I/O parsing boundary: socket/accept threads hand off work to worker pool where first-run cost is higher (initializing tracing/span context, loading per-tenant configs).
4) GC pauses amplified by allocation churn on first N requests, causing tail spikes.

Experiment setup (repro):
- Cluster: 8-vCPU test instance (c5.xlarge equiv) in staging; same code path as prod microservice.
- Workload: wrk2 used to create stepped arrivals: start 10 RPS, step to 50, 100, 200, 400 with 30s holds. Lua script sends a mix of small (1-3 token) and medium (40-60 token) prompts, half with metadata headers.
- Measurements:
  - system: top/htop, mpstat, iostat, free
  - perf: perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -- sleep 20 (during spike)
  - py-spy: py-spy record -o spike.svg --native --pid <pid> --duration 20
  - eBPF: bpftrace one-liners to trace syscalls and lock contention e.g. 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read { @[comm] = count(); }'
  - cProfile on worker entry for micro-run (instrumented only in staging)

Key observations:
1) Timeline: when ramp step hits, incoming request queue length increases almost immediately. CPU climbs to ~85-92% on a single core for the first 1.5-4s, then parallelizes. During that 1-4s window p95 jumps to 180-320ms from baseline ~40ms.
2) py-spy flamegraphs (sampled) show top stacks during spike dominated by: 
   - _socket.recv -> http.server._read_body -> json.loads -> _json.c:parse_string (CPython internal), and
   - request_validation -> re.compile (first call) -> tokenizer.init_bpe_if_missing -> _compile_module
   The traces strongly indicate heavy time in C-backed json parsing (CPython) and Python-level regex compilation on first use.
3) perf (kernel stacks) shows elevated syscalls: epoll_wait (no blocking), futex waits (worker handoffs), and open/mmap during the same window. mmap/open indicate lazy resource initialization (loading certs, opening per-tenant files).
4) cProfile shows a short burst of allocation churn in the request parsing code path leading to increased GC 'collections' activity (seen by gc.get_stats in staging).
5) Threadpool metrics: the default threadpool_size (8) hits full utilization; work is serialized on a small set of threads while others are busy with long initializers (tracing, config fetch).

Interpretation and root causes:
- There is a multi-factor warmup cost: C-level JSON parsing + Python-level regex/BPE initialization + side-effecting initializers (file mappers, KMS clients) that occur lazily on first requests. The combination serializes the early requests and holds the GIL/worker threads long enough to cause queuing and latency spikes.
- Not strictly a tokenizer algorithmic cost problem (the tokenization inner loop is fine once warmed). It's the "first-run" code paths and per-process initialization that dominate.
- GC contributes but is secondary; reducing allocation churn mitigates tail but doesn't remove the initial spike.

Quick wins tried (in staging):
- Pre-import common modules at process start (import json, import regex modules, import tokenizer module). Result: reduced p95 spike magnitude by ~25% in the same workload.
- Warm BPE table into shared mmap at startup (pre-mmap). Result: removed open/mmap flurry; p95 improved another ~15%.
- Replace stdlib json.loads with orjson for parsing request body in a few handler paths. Result: peak CPU on first requests dropped ~30% (orjson is faster in parse-hot paths and uses fewer allocations). Some careful compatibility tests required.
- Pre-compile frequently used regexes (re.compile(...)) at module import time. Result: eliminated re.compile cost from py-spy stacks.

Experiments to run / next steps (ordered):
1) Large-scale warm-start test: run 50 processes with startup-time warmers enabled vs disabled to quantify cluster-level tail improvements. Capture py-spy traces.
2) Convert request validation JSON schema checks to compiled rapidjson/ijson streaming checks to avoid large allocations. Run A/B with orjson and ujson fallbacks and measure correctness differences.
3) Add a small lightweight C-extension or pyo3 shim for BPE init path to move heavy init out of GIL-critical path. Prototype on staging.
4) Add a 'startup pre-warm' hook in our process manager that runs through a small corpus of canonical requests (tenant configs, short prompts) after process start but before routing live traffic. Measure extra startup latency vs request tail improvements. Consider integrating into Dedicated container images as an opt-in start command.
5) Instrument threadpool handoffs: add per-task timestamps (enqueue, dequeue, start_exec) to correlate futex waits with long initialization durations.
6) Investigate replacing per-request KMS client instantiation with a shared pool (KMS client init was causing open/mmap and cert reads under some tenant configs).

Longer-term changes to consider:
- Eager initialization of heavy dependencies in entrypoint (tokenizer tables, regex, KMS, certs), with a lightweight health-check route that ensures warm state before traffic routing.
- Rewrite hot validation paths in Rust (pyo3) to reduce GIL hold times and memory churn.
- Rethink worker model: use a hybrid model where small CPU-heavy parsing runs on a dedicated parsing pool (process or threaded) separate from model-serving threads to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Provide an opt-in config knob for customers to trade a slightly longer cold container start for better burst tail guarantees (pre-warm vs lazy).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How often do tenants trigger different lazy code paths? Some tenants have per-tenant plugin modules that run on first request — need inventory.
- Is orjson safe for all our validation semantics? Edgecases with NaN, big ints, and date handling need validation tests.
- What is the precise GC contribution? Need to run a controlled experiment with tracemalloc and disable GC briefly in staging warmup.

Action items (who/how/when):
- Maya: run full cluster warm-start experiment on staging (50 processes) by 2025-11-21; collect py-spy & perf traces.
- Arjun: prototype a startup pre-warm hook in the systemd/docker entrypoint; measure extra container start time vs warm tail latency by 2025-11-24.
- Sofia: validate orjson compatibility on our largest schema set and open a PR for a partial switch on low-risk routes by 2025-11-28.
- Liam: add lightweight per-task timestamps in request_router (enqueue/dequeue/exec) and add dashboard charts for queue-length and per-stage latency by 2025-11-20.

Notes / reproducibility checklist:
- Wrk script used (attach to linked_artifacts) and exact staging image tag is in JIRA-1784.
- py-spy recorded with --native to capture C extension frames; remember to run as root in staging or use setcap as needed.
- Be careful switching JSON parser in tests: ensure canonical string escaping and number handling is identical.

Appendix: example wrk2 lua snippet used for the stepped workload:
-- wrk-warmup.lua
-- mix of small & medium prompts, random tenant header
request = function()
  local prompts = {"hi", "summarize: short text", string.rep("x", 200)}
  local body = {prompt = prompts[math.random(#prompts)], max_tokens = 64}
  local hdr = {}
  hdr["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
  hdr["X-Tenant-ID"] = "tenant-" .. math.random(1, 10)
  return wrk.format("POST", "/v1/generate", hdr, cjson.encode(body))
end

Flamegraph excerpt (py-spy sampled stack, simplified):
- Thread-1
  - socket.recv
  - http.server._read_body
  - json.loads (CPython)
  - _json.c:parse_string

- Thread-2 (concurrent after ~1.5s)
  - request_validation
  - tokenizer.init_bpe_if_missing
  - re.compile
  - tokenizer.apply_bpe

If anything, this doc is a reminder: many p99 issues are not the tokenization inner loop but the surrounding ecosystem (parsers, initializers, GC, thread handoffs). Focus remediation on warmup and initialization ordering before diving into micro-optimizing the BPE kernel.

Comments welcome — please add findings / alternate hypotheses below.
